newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands to go home to flood-hit Oder region.
newsitem.headline: Thousands to go home to flood-hit Oder region.

text.p: Thousands of people forced from their homes during a flood alert in eastern Germany will be allowed back into the area soon, authorities said on Friday.
About 5,000 people were evacuated from the Oderbruch basin on the swollen River Oder, an area 17 km (11 miles) wide and 50 km (30 miles) long on Germany's frontier with Poland.

Matthias Platzeck, environment minister in the German state of Brandenburg, said water levels along the river were dropping steadily and if this trend continued it would probably be safe enough for most residents to return on Saturday.
Three weeks of the worst flooding in living memory in the region has devastated large tracts of farmland, ruined crops and wrecked villages.

The total damage has yet to be calculated, but officials fear it could run in to billions of marks. Germany has, however, escaped the worst of the floods which killed more than 100 people in the neighbouring Czech Republic and Poland.
Platzeck's ministry said it would cost at least 132 million marks to repair damaged dikes.

Record high river water levels had completely destroyed 3,500 metres (yards) of the 160-km (100-mile) flood barriers, about five km (three miles) of the dikes will need repairs and 28 km (16 miles) of dike paths will have to be rebuilt, the ministry said.

On the other side of the Oder in the Polish town of Slubice, thousands of evacuees returned to their homes two weeks after more than 16,000 of its 18,000 citizens fled potentially catastrophic flooding.
German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt visited the stricken region and reiterated government pledges to help reconstruct after devastation wrought by the worst floods in living memory.

"Now comes the important phase of dealing with the damage and making a new start for the economics ministry...this means providing as much help as possible for suffering businesses," Rexrodt said in the German city of Frankfurt an der Oder, signalling the worst of the crisis was over.

Speaking at a news conference, Platzeck said authorities were still on alert in case the situation changed and he advised against taking the elderly and very young back to the Oderbruch, which is north of Frankfurt an der Oder.

Water levels dropped along the Oder for the fifth consecutive day on Friday and south of Frankfurt an der Oder, in the Ziltendorf basin, where the worst of the German flooding occurred it was falling by one cm (a third of an inch) an hour.
Six villages were partially or totally submerged nearly to the rooftops, about 7,200 hectares (18,000 acres) were engulfed and 300 residents were evacuated.
Many of these areas were still under water and Platzeck said disease-spreading bacteria had reached dangerous levels in stagnant swampy waters.
Health officials have warned residents they could be at risk from typhoid, hepatitis A and bacterial diarrhoea if they come in contact with infected water during the cleanup.
Platzeck said authorities were also trying to clean water polluted by heating oil which has leaked from residents' flooded cellars.
German soldiers continued to monitor the dikes along the Oder, which they have spent the last three weeks trying to reinforce with sandbags, timber logs and gravel.

Donations have poured in for flood-zone victims. Brandenburg's interior minister Alwin Ziel said 55,000 people have donated 7.8 million marks ($4.2 million) so far, according to the Saechsische Zeitung daily.
